title: The Granth's languages
hookLine: Punjabi, saint-speech, Braj and Persian voices, all in one script

cards: Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the letters look steady from page to page: one script, Gurmukhi, running down the lines. Read it aloud, though, and the sound keeps shifting. One hymn rolls in the Punjabi of village fields.
A few pages on, a verse leans toward Persian, the language of courts and clerks. Another carries the old speech of wandering saint-poets. Same letters, different voices.
A child who has learned the alphabet can sound out every line, and still meet words that traveled a long way to get there.

teach.b: Readers who study the Granth hear Punjabi in it, and the shared poetic speech of north Indian saints that scholars call Sant Bhasha, along with Braj, Persian and Arabic words, and verses that lean toward Sanskrit.
The Gurus sang to the people in front of them, and those people spoke in more than one way. Second, one example.

teach.h: YAK ARJ GUFTAM: ONE PLEA BEFORE YOU.
teach.b: In Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak opens a hymn with yak arj guftam, words a Persian speaker would recognize: one plea I make before you. In paraphrase, he asks the Creator to listen, and says this world is passing.
A prayer in the language of the court, set among hymns in the language of the village. Third, other voices. The Granth also holds the hymns of bhagats, saints from outside the line of the Gurus.

teach.h: THE BHAGATS KEEP THEIR OWN VOICES.
teach.b: Sheikh Farid's sloks keep a Punjabi sound of their own. Their words were kept in their own speech, not smoothed into one.
Fourth, the script. All of it is written in Gurmukhi.
Tradition says Guru Angad shaped the script so ordinary people could read the hymns for themselves, with no one standing between them and the Word.
So a child in a gurdwara class on a Sunday morning can sound out Persian, Braj and Punjabi alike. The voices stay different. The letters stay the same.

how: Sikhs learn to read Gurmukhi, often in gurdwara classes, so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves, and the hymns are sung in their original words whatever language they lean toward.

games.q: you're gathering hymns from saints across north India, each in their own speech, into one book. what do you do?
o: translate them all into one language.
keep each voice, and write it all in one script.
leave out anyone who spoke differently.
games.why: the Granth keeps the bhagats' own words, and writes every hymn in Gurmukhi.

practice: On one breath, say softly, or only in your mind, Kartar, the Creator, the name Guru Nanak calls on in his Tilang hymn; on the next, Khuda, a name for God a Persian speaker would know, which the Granth uses too; on the next, Hari, a name from older Indian devotional verse, which the hymns use too.
Let the three sounds sit together, pointing the same way. If you pray, let them be your prayer; if you don't, just notice how each one feels in the mouth.

wordCard.voice: The Granth's languages. Punjabi, Persian, Braj and the speech of the saints, held in a single script, Gurmukhi. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in.
